title: Constructs
overview: Topic 9.2 introduced selection and iteration as ideas for designing an algorithm. This topic is about writing them in exact Cambridge pseudocode and choosing the right one. Paper 2 expects IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF with correct nesting, CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE with single values and ranges, the count-controlled FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT loop, the post-condition REPEAT … UNTIL loop and the pre-condition WHILE … ENDWHILE loop, plus a justified choice of loop for a given problem. Marks are lost for missing ENDIF, ENDCASE or NEXT, for ordering nested IF or CASE clauses so that a later branch can never be reached, for off-by-one FOR bounds, for writing a REPEAT condition as if it were a WHILE condition, and for justifications that only name a loop without linking it to the problem.
syllabusPoints: Use pseudocode to write an 'IF' statement including the 'ELSE' clause and nested IF statements.
Use pseudocode to write a 'CASE' structure, including single values, ranges and an OTHERWISE clause.
Use pseudocode to write a 'count-controlled' loop (FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT).
Use pseudocode to write a 'post-condition' loop (REPEAT … UNTIL).
Use pseudocode to write a 'pre-condition' loop (WHILE … ENDWHILE).
Justify why one loop structure may be better suited to solve a problem than the others.

definitions.definition: A construct in which a condition is evaluated and its result decides which block of statements is executed next; written with IF or CASE.
An IF statement placed inside the THEN or ELSE part of another IF, so that a second condition is tested only after the first has been decided.
A selection construct that compares one expression with a list of values or ranges, executes the statements of the first clause that matches, and uses OTHERWISE for any value that matches none.
Repeating a block of statements, either a set number of times or until a condition is met.
A loop, FOR … NEXT, whose number of repetitions is fixed by a start value, an end value and an optional STEP before the loop begins; the loop variable is updated automatically.
A loop, REPEAT … UNTIL, whose condition is tested after the body, so the body always runs at least once; it stops when the condition becomes TRUE.
A loop, WHILE … ENDWHILE, whose condition is tested before each pass, so the body may run zero times; it continues while the condition is TRUE.
A loop whose ending condition can never be reached, usually because nothing inside the body changes the variables the condition tests.

sections.title: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
content: The simplest selection is IF <condition> THEN <statements> ENDIF. If the condition is TRUE, the statements after THEN run; if it is FALSE they are skipped and execution carries on after ENDIF. Adding an ELSE clause gives a two-way choice: exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both and never neither. The pseudocode guide lays the keywords out on separate lines, with THEN and ELSE indented under IF and the statements indented again; THEN on the same line as the condition is also accepted. Whatever the layout, every IF needs its own ENDIF.

The condition can be any Boolean expression from 11.1: a comparison, a BOOLEAN variable, or a combination joined with AND, OR and NOT. In Python the structure becomes if condition: with an indented block and else: lined up under if, and there is no ENDIF because the indentation ends the block. VB.NET writes If … Then … Else … End If, and Java writes if (condition) { … } else { … }.
bullets: IF … THEN … ENDIF: do something or nothing. IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF: choose between two actions.
Every IF is closed by its own ENDIF, at the same indentation as the IF.
Test a BOOLEAN directly: IF Finished, not IF Finished = TRUE (both are correct, the first is neater).
Python: if … : / else: ; VB.NET: If … Then / Else / End If; Java: if ( … ) { } else { }.

examples.label: IF with and without ELSE
examples.content:
// one-way: nothing happens when the condition is FALSE
IF Temperature > 30
   THEN
      OUTPUT "Heat warning"
ENDIF

// two-way: exactly one branch runs
IF Balance >= Price
   THEN
      Balance ← Balance - Price
      OUTPUT "Purchase complete"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Insufficient funds"
ENDIF

sections.title: Nested IF statements
content: An IF can be placed inside the THEN or the ELSE block of another IF. The inner test is only reached when the outer test has already gone a particular way, so the inner condition can rely on what the outer one has established. A login check is a natural case: there is no point testing the password until the username has been found, and the two failures need different messages. Each inner IF must be completely closed with its own ENDIF before the outer IF continues, so an IF nested twice ends with two ENDIFs.

Nesting in the ELSE branch builds a chain of tests on the same value, such as 'if negative … else if zero … else …'. Here the order of the tests matters: the first condition that is TRUE wins, so tests must go from the most specific or most extreme case outward. Python shortens an ELSE-then-IF into elif, and VB.NET into ElseIf, each needing only one closing keyword; in pseudocode you still write the full ELSE, IF and ENDIF. When every branch compares the same single variable with fixed values or ranges, a CASE structure is usually clearer.
bullets: The inner IF runs only on one path of the outer IF.
Count your ENDIFs: one per IF, closed innermost first.
In an ELSE-IF chain, test the most restrictive condition first, or later branches become unreachable.
Use nested IF when different conditions or different variables are involved; use CASE for one variable against many values.

examples.label: Nested IF: a two-stage login check
examples.content:
IF Username = StoredName
   THEN
      IF Password = StoredPassword
         THEN
            OUTPUT "Welcome ", Username
         ELSE
            OUTPUT "Wrong password"
      ENDIF
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Unknown user"
ENDIF

// StoredName "kim", StoredPassword "Tr33top"
// Username "kim", Password "Tr33top"  → Welcome kim
// Username "kim", Password "treetop"  → Wrong password
// Username "sam", any password        → Unknown user (the password is never tested)

sections.title: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
content: A CASE structure compares the value of one expression, usually a single variable, with a list of clauses. Each clause is a value, or a range written <low> TO <high>, followed by a colon and the statement to run. The clauses are checked from the top, and only the first clause that matches is executed; after that, control jumps past ENDCASE. The optional final clause, OTHERWISE, runs when nothing above it matched, which makes it the natural place for an error message about invalid data. The coursebook also shows several values separated by commas in one clause, which VB.NET supports directly.

Ranges suit INTEGER and CHAR values, for example 70 TO 100 or 'A' TO 'Z'. Because the first match wins, overlapping ranges are legal but the later part of an overlap is never reached, so ranges should normally be written so that they do not overlap. A REAL value such as 69.5 would fall between two whole-number ranges, so either round it first or use nested IF with < and >= tests instead. Python has no CASE statement in older versions and is normally translated into if … elif … else; Python 3.10's match statement handles single values but not ranges. VB.NET uses Select Case with Case 70 To 100 and Case Else, and Java uses switch with case labels, break and default.
bullets: CASE OF <identifier> … ENDCASE; each clause is <value> : <statement> or <low> TO <high> : <statement>.
Only the first matching clause runs, so clause order matters when values could match more than one.
OTHERWISE catches every unlisted value; use it to reject invalid input.
A CASE tests one expression only; conditions on different variables need IF.

examples.label: CASE with ranges: converting a mark to a grade
examples.content:
DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
DECLARE Grade : STRING
INPUT Mark
CASE OF Mark
   70 TO 100 : Grade ← "Distinction"
   50 TO 69  : Grade ← "Merit"
   40 TO 49  : Grade ← "Pass"
   0 TO 39   : Grade ← "Fail"
   OTHERWISE : Grade ← "Invalid mark"
ENDCASE
OUTPUT Grade

Test data (normal, boundary and erroneous)
Mark | Clause matched | OUTPUT
73   | 70 TO 100      | Distinction
70   | 70 TO 100      | Distinction
69   | 50 TO 69       | Merit
40   | 40 TO 49       | Pass
39   | 0 TO 39        | Fail
105  | OTHERWISE      | Invalid mark
-3   | OTHERWISE      | Invalid mark

examples.label: CASE with single character values
examples.content:
INPUT Choice
CASE OF UCASE(Choice)
   'A' : OUTPUT "Adding a record"
   'D' : OUTPUT "Deleting a record"
   'S' : OUTPUT "Searching"
   OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Not a menu option"
ENDCASE

// Choice 'd' → UCASE gives 'D' → Deleting a record
// Choice 'x' → Not a menu option

sections.title: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
content: A FOR loop repeats its body a number of times that is fixed before the first pass. It is written FOR <identifier> ← <start> TO <end>, followed by the body and then NEXT <identifier>. The loop variable is given the start value, the body runs, the variable is increased by 1, and this repeats until the pass with the end value has been completed. FOR Count ← 1 TO 5 therefore runs five times, with Count taking 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. For a start of 1, the number of passes is simply the end value; in general, with the default step it is End - Start + 1.

STEP changes the amount added each time: FOR X ← 2 TO 14 STEP 4 gives 2, 6, 10 and 14, and a negative step counts down, so FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3 gives 10, 7, 4 and 1. The loop stops once the next value would pass the end value, so the end value itself is only used if the steps land on it exactly. The pseudocode guide requires the step to be a whole number, and the body must not assign to the loop variable. Python's range excludes its end value, which is the usual source of off-by-one errors when translating: FOR X ← 1 TO 5 becomes for x in range(1, 6), and FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3 becomes range(10, 0, -3). A FOR loop is also the natural way to visit every element of an array or every character of a string, as in FOR Position ← 1 TO LENGTH(Word).
bullets: FOR … NEXT for a known number of passes; NEXT names the same loop variable as FOR.
Default step is +1; STEP -1 counts down; the step must be an integer.
Never change the loop variable inside the body.
Python: range(start, end + 1, step) for a counting-up loop, because range stops before its end value.

examples.label: Trace: two FOR loops using STEP
examples.content:
Total ← 0
FOR N ← 2 TO 10 STEP 2
   Total ← Total + N
NEXT N
OUTPUT Total

N  | Total
   | 0
2  | 2
4  | 6
6  | 12
8  | 20
10 | 30      → OUTPUT 30 (5 passes: the even numbers 2 to 10)

FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3
   OUTPUT X
NEXT X

X  | OUTPUT
10 | 10
7  | 7
4  | 4
1  | 1       → next value would be -2, which is past 1, so the loop ends

Python check: sum(range(2, 11, 2)) = 30 and list(range(10, 0, -3)) = [10, 7, 4, 1].

sections.title: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
content: A REPEAT loop runs its body first and tests the condition afterwards: REPEAT <statements> UNTIL <condition>. If the condition is FALSE, the body runs again; as soon as it is TRUE, the loop ends. Because the test comes at the end, the body always runs at least once. This makes REPEAT the natural choice for input validation, where a value has to be read before there is anything to check, and for menus that must be shown at least once.

The condition describes when to stop, so it is the opposite of a WHILE condition for the same task: UNTIL LENGTH(Code) = 4 means the same as WHILE LENGTH(Code) <> 4. Something inside the body must be able to make the condition TRUE, usually an INPUT or an update to a counter, or the loop will never end. Python has no post-condition loop; the usual translation is while True: with the body followed by if condition: break. VB.NET writes Do … Loop Until condition and Java writes do { … } while (!condition);, where Java's condition is reversed because it says when to continue.
bullets: Body first, test last: at least one pass is guaranteed.
UNTIL gives the stopping condition; the loop repeats while it is FALSE.
No variable in the condition needs a value before the loop, as long as the body sets it.
Python: while True: … if condition: break.

examples.label: Trace: REPEAT until a 4-character code is entered
examples.content:
DECLARE Code : STRING
REPEAT
   OUTPUT "Enter a 4-character code: "
   INPUT Code
UNTIL LENGTH(Code) = 4
OUTPUT "Code accepted: ", Code

Inputs: "12", "12345", "7a9b"
Pass | Code    | LENGTH(Code) | LENGTH(Code) = 4 ? | Action
1    | "12"    | 2            | FALSE              | repeat
2    | "12345" | 5            | FALSE              | repeat
3    | "7a9b"  | 4            | TRUE               | leave loop
OUTPUT: the prompt three times, then Code accepted: 7a9b

sections.title: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
content: A WHILE loop tests its condition before every pass: WHILE <condition> <statements> ENDWHILE. If the condition is TRUE the body runs and the test is made again; as soon as it is FALSE, execution continues after ENDWHILE. If the condition is already FALSE the first time, the body is skipped completely, so a WHILE loop can run zero times. The current pseudocode guide writes WHILE <condition> on its own; the coursebook adds DO at the end of the line, and either is understood.

Every variable in the condition must already have a value when the loop is first reached, so a WHILE loop is usually preceded by an initialising assignment or a first INPUT. As with REPEAT, the body must change something the condition depends on. WHILE suits problems where the loop may legitimately not be needed at all, such as processing data that might be empty, or repeating a calculation until a target is reached when the target might already be met. Python, VB.NET and Java all have this loop directly: while condition:, Do While … Loop and while (condition) { }.
bullets: Test first, body second: zero or more passes.
WHILE gives the condition to carry on; the loop ends when it becomes FALSE.
Initialise the condition's variables before the loop.
Make sure the body can eventually make the condition FALSE.

examples.label: Trace: smallest power of 2 that is at least N
examples.content:
DECLARE N, Power, Doublings : INTEGER
INPUT N
Power ← 1
Doublings ← 0
WHILE Power < N
   Power ← Power * 2
   Doublings ← Doublings + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Power, " after ", Doublings, " doublings"

N = 37
Power | Doublings | Power < 37 ?
1     | 0         | TRUE
2     | 1         | TRUE
4     | 2         | TRUE
8     | 3         | TRUE
16    | 4         | TRUE
32    | 5         | TRUE
64    | 6         | FALSE → OUTPUT 64 after 6 doublings

N = 1
Power | Doublings | Power < 1 ?
1     | 0         | FALSE → body never runs, OUTPUT 1 after 0 doublings

A REPEAT version would double at least once and wrongly output 2 for N = 1.

sections.title: Justifying the choice of loop
content: Any loop can be rewritten using either of the others, so the question is which fits the problem best. Ask two things. First, is the number of passes known when the loop is reached, even if it is held in a variable such as ClassSize or LENGTH(Word)? If so, use FOR: the counting is built in, so there is no counter to initialise or increment and no condition to get wrong. Second, if the number is not known, must the body run at least once? If yes, use REPEAT … UNTIL; if the body might not be needed at all, use WHILE … ENDWHILE.

A justification earns marks when it links the property of the loop to the specific problem, not when it just names the loop. 'REPEAT, because the password has to be entered before it can be checked, so the body must run at least once' scores; 'REPEAT, because it is a condition-controlled loop' does not. For a FOR loop the key phrase is 'the number of iterations is known before the loop starts'; for WHILE it is 'the condition is tested first, so the loop can be skipped when it is not needed'.
bullets: Known number of passes → FOR (count-controlled).
Unknown, but at least one pass needed → REPEAT … UNTIL (post-condition).
Unknown, and zero passes possible → WHILE … ENDWHILE (pre-condition).
Always tie the justification to the scenario, not just to the definition.

examples.label: Worked example: one task written three ways, and three justified choices
examples.content:
Output the numbers 1 to 5

FOR Count ← 1 TO 5         Count ← 1                  Count ← 1
   OUTPUT Count            REPEAT                     WHILE Count <= 5
NEXT Count                    OUTPUT Count               OUTPUT Count
                              Count ← Count + 1          Count ← Count + 1
                           UNTIL Count > 5            ENDWHILE

All three output 1 2 3 4 5, but FOR needs no manual initialise-and-increment, so it is the best fit.
Note the conditions: WHILE Count <= 5 (carry on) is the opposite of UNTIL Count > 5 (stop).

Scenario                                              Best loop and justification
Total the marks of the 30 students in a class         FOR: the number of iterations (30) is known
                                                      before the loop starts.
Keep asking for a PIN until it is 4 digits long       REPEAT: a PIN must be input before it can
                                                      be checked, so the body must run at least once.
Print every line of a file, which may be empty        WHILE NOT EOF(…): the test comes first, so an
                                                      empty file is handled with zero passes.

sections.title: Combining and nesting constructs
content: Real programs place constructs inside one another: an IF or CASE inside a loop to treat each value differently, a loop inside a loop to cover rows and columns, or a validation loop inside a counting loop. The inner construct runs completely on every pass of the outer one, and each construct keeps its own closing keyword at the matching indentation: ENDIF, ENDCASE, NEXT, UNTIL or ENDWHILE. Closing keywords must be nested properly, so an ENDIF that belongs inside a FOR loop has to appear before that loop's NEXT.

To trace nested constructs, add a column for every variable and for the output, and work through the inner construct fully for each value of the outer loop variable before moving on. The example below uses a FOR loop containing a nested IF chain. It also shows why order matters: a number divisible by 15 is also divisible by 3 and by 5, so the MOD 15 test has to come first or that branch would never run.
bullets: Inner constructs complete on every pass of the outer loop.
Close constructs innermost first: an inner ENDIF comes before the outer NEXT.
Indent each level consistently so the structure can be checked by eye.
In an IF chain inside a loop, put the most specific test first.

examples.label: Trace: nested IF inside a FOR loop
examples.content:
FOR Number ← 9 TO 15
   IF Number MOD 15 = 0
      THEN
         OUTPUT "FizzBuzz"
      ELSE
         IF Number MOD 3 = 0
            THEN
               OUTPUT "Fizz"
            ELSE
               IF Number MOD 5 = 0
                  THEN
                     OUTPUT "Buzz"
                  ELSE
                     OUTPUT Number
               ENDIF
         ENDIF
   ENDIF
NEXT Number

Number | MOD 15 | MOD 3 | MOD 5 | OUTPUT
9      | 9      | 0     | –     | Fizz
10     | 10     | 1     | 0     | Buzz
11     | 11     | 2     | 1     | 11
12     | 12     | 0     | –     | Fizz
13     | 13     | 1     | 3     | 13
14     | 14     | 2     | 4     | 14
15     | 0      | –     | –     | FizzBuzz
(– means the test is not reached)

diagram.title: Choosing a loop structure
nodes: Is the number of repetitions known when the loop is reached?
No → must the body run at least once?
Yes → REPEAT … UNTIL (condition tested after the body)
No → WHILE … ENDWHILE (condition tested before the body; may run zero times)
Check: something in the body changes the condition, so the loop ends

analysisChains.title: A nested IF whose last branch can never run
steps: A candidate grades marks with IF Mark >= 40 THEN "Pass" ELSE IF Mark >= 70 THEN "Distinction" …
Any mark of 70 or more also satisfies Mark >= 40, so it takes the first branch
The Mark >= 70 test sits in the ELSE branch, which is only reached by marks below 40, so it can never be TRUE
Reordering to test Mark >= 70 first, then Mark >= 40, or using CASE with non-overlapping ranges, fixes it
analysisChains.evaluation: Selection takes the first TRUE branch. In a chain of tests on one value, the most restrictive condition must come first; a test table with the boundary values 39, 40, 69 and 70 exposes the error immediately.

analysisChains.title: Translating a WHILE loop into REPEAT … UNTIL
steps: A WHILE loop reads WHILE Power < N … ENDWHILE and must be rewritten as a post-condition loop
UNTIL states when to stop, so the condition is negated: UNTIL Power >= N
Tracing N = 37 gives the same result, 64 after 6 doublings, because the WHILE body ran at least once anyway
Tracing N = 1 shows a difference: WHILE outputs 1 after 0 doublings, but REPEAT doubles once and outputs 2 after 1 doubling
analysisChains.evaluation: Swapping loop types means reversing the condition and checking the zero-pass case. When zero passes is a valid outcome, only a pre-condition loop (or an extra IF around a REPEAT) gives the right answer.

analysisChains.title: Justifying FOR over WHILE for an array total
steps: A program must add up the 30 values in Scores[1:30]
The number of passes, 30, is fixed before the loop starts
A WHILE version needs Index ← 1 before the loop, WHILE Index <= 30, and Index ← Index + 1 inside; forgetting the increment gives an infinite loop, and writing < 30 misses the last value
FOR Index ← 1 TO 30 … NEXT Index sets, tests and updates Index automatically
analysisChains.evaluation: Because the number of iterations is known in advance, a count-controlled loop is the better choice: it is shorter and removes the chance of a missing increment or an off-by-one condition. Conditional loops are for when that number is not known.

examTips: Close every construct: IF with ENDIF, CASE OF with ENDCASE, FOR with NEXT <same identifier>, REPEAT with UNTIL, WHILE with ENDWHILE.
Indent each level of nesting so the examiner can see which ENDIF belongs to which IF.
In CASE, check that ranges do not overlap and add OTHERWISE for invalid values.
Remember REPEAT stops when its condition is TRUE, WHILE stops when its condition is FALSE; reverse the condition when converting between them.
To justify a loop, name it and link its property to the scenario: known number of iterations (FOR), must run at least once (REPEAT), may not need to run at all (WHILE).
commonMistakes: Forgetting ENDIF on an inner IF, so that later statements are wrongly inside or outside the selection.
Putting the broadest test first in an IF chain or CASE, making later branches unreachable.
Writing FOR Count ← 1 TO 9 when ten passes were needed, or translating it to Python as range(1, 9).
Using the WHILE condition after UNTIL (UNTIL Count <= 5 instead of UNTIL Count > 5).
Leaving a WHILE or REPEAT loop without any statement that changes its condition, causing an infinite loop, or using a WHILE condition variable that has no value yet.
Changing the FOR loop variable inside the loop body.

quickRecall.question: Write the skeleton of a two-way selection in Cambridge pseudocode.
quickRecall.answer: IF <condition> THEN <statements> ELSE <statements> ENDIF, with THEN and ELSE on their own indented lines.

quickRecall.question: In a CASE structure, what happens when a value matches two clauses, and what is OTHERWISE for?
quickRecall.answer: Only the first matching clause runs. OTHERWISE runs when no clause matches, typically to report invalid data.

quickRecall.question: What values does FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3 give X, and what is the Python equivalent?
What is the minimum number of times the body of a REPEAT loop and of a WHILE loop can run?
quickRecall.answer: REPEAT at least once (condition tested after the body); WHILE zero times (condition tested before the body).

quickRecall.question: Rewrite WHILE Total < 100 … ENDWHILE as a post-condition loop condition.
quickRecall.answer: REPEAT … UNTIL Total >= 100 (the condition is reversed, and the body now runs at least once).

quickRecall.question: When is a FOR loop the best choice?
quickRecall.answer: When the number of iterations is known when the loop is reached, for example the size of an array or a value already input.

quickRecall.question: Justify using REPEAT … UNTIL to validate an input.
quickRecall.answer: The value has to be input before it can be checked, so the body must execute at least once; REPEAT tests its condition after the body, guaranteeing that first pass.

quickRecall.question: Why must an inner IF inside a FOR loop have its ENDIF before the loop's NEXT?
quickRecall.answer: Constructs must be closed innermost first; the IF is part of the loop body, so it has to finish before the loop does.
